procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 24th December, 1953, of the Election Tribunal, Gwalior, Madhya Bharat, in Election Petition No. 263 of 1952.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeals by Special Leave against the Judgment and Order

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails in so far as it attacks the Tribunal's declaration voiding the election of the' two appellants but succeeds against that part of the order which declares tl1e 6th and 7th respondents to have been elected.
directions: There will be no order about costs in either Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether sections 123(5) and 124(5) of the Representation of the People Act (XLIII of 1951) are ultra vires Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellants challenged sections 123(5) and 124(5) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

They argued that these sections, which define certain actions like systematic appeals to caste as corrupt practices, violated their fundamental right to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
law: The Supreme Court distinguished between a fundamental right and a statutory right.
The right to stand as a candidate and contest an election is not a common law or fundamental right, but a special right created by statute.
A statutory right can only be exercised on the conditions laid down by the statute that creates it.
application: The Court reasoned that the Fundamental Rights chapter of the Constitution does not have a bearing on a statutory right like contesting an election.
The challenged sections do not stop a person from speaking in general. They merely prescribe the conditions that must be observed if one wants to become a Member of Parliament.
If the appellants wish to exercise their right of free speech without these restrictions, they are free to do so, but they cannot simultaneously seek to be elected under the rules they are violating.
Therefore, the appellants have no fundamental right to be elected, and if they want to be, they must follow the rules laid down by the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that sections 123(5) and 124(5) of the Representation of the People Act are not ultra vires Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution because they are valid conditions attached to the statutory right to contest an election, not an unconstitutional restriction on the fundamental right to free speech.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was justified in declaring the election of the two appellants to be void.

facts.fact: The Election Tribunal found that the first appellant committed a 'major corrupt practice' by publishing pamphlets containing false statements about a rival candidate's personal character and conduct.
The Tribunal found that the second appellant's election was 'procured by a corrupt practice'.
The Tribunal also found that both appellants committed an 'illegal practice' by issuing a leaflet and poster that did not have the printer's name on them.

law.law: Under section 100(2)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, if a Tribunal finds that a corrupt practice has been committed, it shall declare the election of the returned candidate to be void.
Under section 100(2)(a), an election is void if it has been 'procured or induced' by any corrupt or illegal practice.
When a corrupt practice is proven under section 100(2)(b), it is not necessary to also prove that the result of the election was materially affected.

application.application: The Court upheld the Tribunal's finding that the first appellant committed a corrupt practice. It treated this as a finding of fact and declined to re-examine it on special appeal, stating the Tribunal's conclusion was one that 'judicial minds could reasonably reach'.
Because the first appellant was found to have committed a corrupt practice, the Court held that under section 100(2)(b), the Tribunal was justified in declaring his election void.

The Court accepted the Tribunal's finding that the second appellant's election was procured by a corrupt practice. This fell squarely within the first part of section 100(2)(a), making it unnecessary to inquire further.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Election Tribunal was justified in declaring the elections of both appellants void. The first appellant's election was voided due to the commission of a corrupt practice (publishing false statements), and the second appellant's election was voided because it was procured by a corrupt practice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was justified in declaring the 6th and 7th respondents to have been duly elected.

facts: The Election Tribunal, after voiding the elections of the 1st and 2nd respondents due to corrupt practices, declared the 6th and 7th respondents to have been duly elected.
For the General Constituency, the 1st respondent had 13,669 votes and the 6th respondent had 12,750 votes.
For the Scheduled Caste seat, the 2nd respondent had 12,452 votes and the 7th respondent had 10,889 votes.
The Tribunal concluded that if not for the corrupt practices, the 6th and 7th respondents would have undoubtedly obtained a majority of valid votes.
law: To declare a candidate duly elected in place of a disqualified candidate, it must be proved that "but for the votes obtained by the returned candidate by corrupt or illegal practices.... such other candidate would have obtained a majority of the valid votes."
application: The Supreme Court found the Tribunal's reasoning to be "pure speculation" and not a conclusion a reasonable mind could reach based on the data.
The Court noted there was no evidence to show why voters who chose the 1st respondent would have preferred the 6th respondent over the 3rd and 4th respondents.
Similarly, there was no basis to conclude that those who voted for the 2nd respondent would have preferred the 7th respondent over the 5th respondent.
The Tribunal failed to provide the necessary proof and instead made an unsupported assumption that the votes for the disqualified candidates would automatically transfer to the runners-up.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Tribunal's decision, holding that it was wrong to declare the 6th and 7th respondents as duly elected. The Tribunal's conclusion was based on speculation rather than the required proof that these candidates would have secured a majority of valid votes in the absence of the corrupt practices.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sections 123(5) and 124(5) of the Representation of the People Act (XLIII of 1951) are ultra vires Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: Sections 123(5) and 124(5) of the Representation of the People Act are unconstitutional as they interfere with a citizen's fundamental right to freedom of speech, as guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The laws are constitutional as they do not prevent a citizen from speaking, but rather prescribe conditions for those who wish to stand for election, which is not a fundamental right.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was justified in declaring the election of the two appellants to be void.
appellant_arguments: The Tribunal's findings were incorrect; the statements made against the 6th respondent were a legitimate attack on his public and political character, not his personal character.
They contested the finding that the corrupt practices materially affected the result of the election.
respondent_arguments: The Tribunal was justified because the first appellant committed a major corrupt practice under section 123(5) by publishing false statements about the personal character and conduct of the 6th respondent.
The second appellant committed a minor corrupt practice under section 124(5) by making a systematic appeal to voters on the basis of his caste.
Under section 100(2)(b), the commission of any corrupt practice is sufficient to void the election, and it is not necessary to prove that the result was materially affected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was justified in declaring the 6th and 7th respondents to have been duly elected.
appellant_arguments: The Tribunal was wrong to declare the 6th and 7th respondents elected, as its conclusion was based on 'pure speculation' and not on proof.
There was no evidence to show that 'but for' the corrupt practices, the voters would have preferred the 6th and 7th respondents over other candidates.
respondent_arguments: The Tribunal was justified in its declaration.

Given the scandalous nature of the corrupt practices and the narrow margin of votes, it was a reasonable conclusion that respondents 6 and 7 would have obtained a majority of valid votes if the corrupt practices had not occurred.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The right to stand as a candidate and contest an election is a statutory right, not a common law or fundamental right, and can only be exercised on the conditions laid down by the governing statute. Consequently, statutory provisions that regulate the conduct of candidates, such as those prohibiting certain corrupt practices, do not violate the fundamental right to freedom of speech. The commission of a corrupt practice by a returned candidate is sufficient to declare their election void; it is not necessary to also prove that the result of the election was materially affected by that practice. Furthermore, to declare another candidate as duly elected after an election is voided, it must be proven that this other candidate would have obtained a majority of the valid votes but for the votes obtained by the returned candidate through corrupt or illegal practices.
obiter: It is not necessary to determine if a corrupt practice materially affected the result of an election when the case falls under a statutory alternative where the mere commission of the practice is sufficient to void the election.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court upheld the Election Tribunal's decision to void the appellants' elections due to proven corrupt practices, but overturned the part of the order that declared the 6th and 7th respondents as the duly elected candidates. The court found that while the commission of a corrupt practice automatically invalidates the election of the perpetrator under the Representation of the People Act, declaring another candidate as the winner requires positive proof that they would have secured a majority of valid votes 'but for' the corrupt practices. The Tribunal's conclusion on this latter point was deemed to be 'pure speculation' and not a conclusion a reasonable mind could judicially reach based on the evidence.
legal_tests_applied: Constitutionality of Election Laws vs. Fundamental Rights: The right to stand as a candidate and contest an election is not a common law right but a special right created by statute, which can be exercised only on the conditions laid down by that statute, and the Fundamental Rights Chapter has no bearing on such a right.

Voiding an Election for Corrupt Practices (Section 100(2)(b)): The commission of any corrupt practice is sufficient to declare the election of the candidate void, and it is not necessary to prove that the result of the election was materially affected thereby.

Declaring a Runner-up as Elected (Section 101(b)): To declare a candidate other than the returned candidate as elected, it must be proved that 'but for the votes obtained by the returned candidate by corrupt or illegal practices .... such other candidate would have obtained a majority of the valid votes.'

Standard of Review on Special Appeal: The court will not examine the Tribunal's factual findings as a Court of appeal but will only interfere when there is some glaring error which has resulted in a substantial miscarriage of justice or when the conclusion is one that no tribunal of reasonable and unbiased men could judicially reach.
why_appellant_lost: The constitutional challenge to sections 123(5) and 124(5) of the Representation of the People Act failed because the right to stand for election is a statutory right, not a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a). The court reasoned: 'These laws do not stop a man from speaking. They merely prescribe conditions which must be observed if he wants to enter Parliament... If they want that they must observe the rules.'

The court refused to overturn the Tribunal's factual finding that the appellants committed corrupt practices. Applying a limited standard of review, the court held that the Tribunal's conclusion that the first appellant attacked the respondent's personal character and that the second appellant appealed to caste was one 'which judicial minds could reasonably reach.'

The argument that the corrupt practices did not materially affect the election result was dismissed as irrelevant for voiding the election. The court clarified that under section 100(2)(b), 'All that need be proved is that a corrupt practice has been committed,' which makes the election void without needing to prove its effect on the outcome.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the election laws were constitutional was accepted. The court affirmed that the right to contest an election is a special right created by statute, and the conditions imposed by these laws, such as prohibiting certain types of speech during a campaign, do not infringe upon the fundamental right to freedom of speech.

The respondent's position that the appellants' elections were rightly voided was upheld. The court agreed with the Tribunal's finding of corrupt practices and affirmed the legal principle that under Section 100(2)(b), the commission of such a practice is, by itself, sufficient grounds to declare the election of the returned candidate to be void.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the policy that the right to participate in the electoral process as a candidate is a privilege governed by statute, which carries with it a responsibility to adhere to a code of conduct designed to ensure fair elections.

The judgment upholds the principle of finality for the factual findings of specialized bodies like Election Tribunals, with the Supreme Court intervening only in cases of glaring error or manifest injustice, thereby respecting the statutory scheme.

The court established a high evidentiary bar for judicially altering an election outcome by declaring a runner-up as the winner. Requiring concrete proof under the 'but for' test, rather than allowing 'pure speculation', protects the integrity of the electoral result and prevents the judiciary from conjecturing the will of the voters.
